10754-little-sarah:
Little Sarah is a small picture book in verse for young children, from the "New Colored Toys" series. Sarah stands by her grandmother's bed and is sent to make a johnny-cake, mixed in one minute and baked in two. The meal barrel is empty, the shopkeeper has none, and Sarah must run to the miller to have corn ground in a minute.

The rhymes follow her errand step by step, with pictures to match, teaching patience and helpfulness through a simple task. The verse is plain and rhythmic, made to be read aloud. Families get a charming period nursery book, short enough for bedtime and easy for children to follow.
16503-another-world-fragments-from-the-s:
Writing as Hermes, the author of this 1873 book offers fragments from Montalluyah, a star city on another world. The preface cites Brewster and Proctor on the plurality of worlds, then promises an account of one star world's customs and moral state. Chapters treat Montalluyah itself, Vyora, perseverance, and the narrator's labors and triumph.

The book mixes utopian fancy with moral argument, asking whether men can be brought to seek knowledge as ardently as money. Its fragment form keeps the wonders brief and strange. Readers of early science fiction will find a curious Victorian vision of life beyond Earth.
20766-the-autobiography-of-methuselah:
A joke on damning the rain opens The Autobiography of Methuselah, from 1908. The teller weighs whether the wish means endless doom or a mere dam in the way. Such wordplay fits a life stretched across near a thousand years of Bible time.

John Kendrick Bangs, a famed humor writer, lends Methuselah his wit. The old man looks back on Adam, Noah, and a world grown young around him. Tall talk and gentle mockery fill the tale. Readers get a light, clever spin on the oldest man in scripture, told as if he wrote his own life at last.
21320-mass-george-a-boy-s-adventures-in-:
George Bruton, a young teenager on his father's Georgia plantation in the mid-eighteenth century, narrates George Manville Fenn's tale of the old Savannah. Captain Bruton, uneasy about slavery, buys an enslaved man and resolves to treat him well. The man's son joins the household, and the family nicknames him Pompey, or Pomp.

George and Pomp become fast friends through adventures with alligators, floods, fire, snakes, ants, and attacks by Native peoples and Spaniards from Florida. Much of the book is talk between the two boys. After the pair behave well through a long series of attacks, Captain Bruton decides to free both father and son.
21364-the-rajah-of-dah:
Ned, sixteen and fresh from school, begs to join his naturalist uncle's next expedition in George Manville Fenn's tale of Burma. They travel upriver past the trading port of Dindong to a British settlement under a British protectorate. The local ruler, the Rajah of Dah, proves an absurd and loathsome tyrant.

Ned and his English friend Frank catch an eighteen-foot crocodile among their adventures. Trouble sharpens when the Rajah sets his eye on a young British woman of the settlement for his harem. Fenn then turns the river journey into a rescue tale, with the settlement's quarrel with the Rajah coming to a head.
21485-the-young-rajah:
A young man sails to India in search of his father's papers in W. H. G. Kingston's The Young Rajah. The time is just before the Indian Mutiny, and unrest stirs across the land. His ship, the Glamorgan Castle, carries him to the Hooghly and a fateful meeting.

In the Rajah's territory, where his father once served, troubles break out around him. Slowly it emerges that the youth is the old Rajah's grandson and heir. The honour sits ill with him, since crowds treat him with awe. Shipboard love, a gallant rescue, and brisk action keep the tale moving well.
22663-a-ghetto-violet-from-christian-and:
Leopold Kompert wrote A Ghetto Violet, drawn from his novel Christian and Leah, a story of Jewish village life in Bohemia. The catalog record gives no year. Kompert was among the first writers to portray the ghetto from inside, with warmth and close knowledge of its customs.

In the sample, Ephraim refuses to sell or give away a caged bird, answering his sister's excitement with quiet calm. He would do nothing to pain her, he says, yet one word from him would make her open the cage herself and bid the bird fly home. The bird plainly stands for a human hope or bond. Kompert's gentle scenes preserve a world of faith, family pressure, and small freedoms that later history erased.
22749-from-edinburgh-to-india-burmah:
W. G. Burn Murdoch wrote From Edinburgh to India and Burmah, a travel narrative by the Scottish artist and explorer. The catalog record gives no year. Burn Murdoch sailed and sketched his way from Scotland to the East, and his book mixes voyage, pageantry, and the politics of empire.

The sample chapter deals with splendid royal shows in India. It even pauses for a curious dream: a prince and an aide-de-camp correct the abuses of the Royal Academies' privileges. Such whimsy sits beside durbar splendor and Burmese scenes in Burn Murdoch's manner. He writes as a painter talks: color first, commentary close behind. The book is a lively period record of the route from Edinburgh to Rangoon.
22843-aunt-deborah:
A hard family history stands behind Aunt Deborah, a story by Mary Russell Mitford. A clerk's son was driven from his father's door, tried, failed, and finally died broken-hearted. His widow, rosy-cheeked no longer, was driven off in her turn with her little boy. The old man kept his property close to the end.

When he died, within a year or two, he left everything to his daughter Deborah. That bequest makes Deborah the aunt of the title and the center of the tale. Mitford traces what money, grievance, and duty do inside one family across years. The story is sadder than her usual sketches. It shows her range, from comedy of manners into quiet tragedy.
23688-the-indulgence-of-negu-mah:
Robert Arthur published this science fiction story in Comet magazine in July 1941. Its hero is Negu Mah, a uranium merchant of Callisto. He sits in his garden under a shell of pure vitrite, sipping molkai with his guest Sliss, an amphibian from the swamps of Venus.

Negu Mah's wife Nanlo serves them as Jupiter rises over the horizon, and the slim shaft of the cargo rocket Vulcan stands ready, newest and swiftest of his freighter fleet. What begins as a leisurely visit among traders turns on the merchant's indulgence — a weakness, a wish, or a luxury that carries a price. Arthur tells it with color, humor, and a vivid sense of life across the solar system.
2478-the-circus-boys-on-the-plains-or-th:
Edgar B. P. Darlington sends his Circus Boys onto the plains as young advance agents, drumming up crowds for the show ahead of its arrival. The story follows the boys through prairie towns, where they post bills, dodge rivals, and learn the business side of the circus. The plains setting gives the adventure a western flavor.

The book's charm lies in its mix of showmanship and frontier travel. Young readers will enjoy the boys' growing responsibility. It stands as a sturdy middle volume of the series. Advance agents traveled ahead of the circus to plaster towns with posters.
30899-the-man-who-did-not-die-the-story-:
J. H. Willard wrote this retelling of the story of Elijah, published by Henry Altemus in Philadelphia in 1906 as part of Altemus' Beautiful Stories series, each volume selling for twenty-five cents. The series pairs it with The First Christmas, The First Easter, The Story of Solomon, The Story of Ruth, The Story of Elisha, and The Story of Samson. Willard tells the Bible story in plain, illustrated prose for young readers.

The book opens after the death of King Solomon, when his son Rehoboam becomes ruler of the Israelites. Heavy taxation to pay for Solomon's lavish court has left the people discontented and disloyal, and Rehoboam, following his younger counsellors, scornfully rejects their petition to lighten their burdens. Against that troubled kingdom, Elijah's story unfolds. It is a short, clear Bible tale, told for children.
34340-three-new-beavers-from-utah:
Three New Beavers from Utah is a short zoology paper by Stephen Durrant and Harold Crane. The University of Kansas put it out in its Museum of Natural History series on December 24, 1948. It runs from page 407 to page 417, with seven figures. The pair worked from beaver specimens held at the University of Utah.

Older writers had lumped Utah beavers under one name from Mexico. Close study of skins and skulls showed far more variety than that. Durrant and Crane name and describe three new subspecies, each with a type specimen, a range, and full measurements. They warn that moving beavers between streams could blur such kinds. Field workers get a careful base for telling Utah beavers apart.
34449-a-new-extinct-emydid-turtle-from-t:
Edwin Galbreath's paper on a new extinct emydid turtle from the Lower Pliocene of Oklahoma appeared in August 1948. It ran in the University of Kansas Publications, Museum of Natural History, volume one, number sixteen, pages 265 to 280, with one plate. The plate shows the new form's shell from above and below.

In the summer of 1946, Galbreath writes, a party from the Kansas museum visited the Laverne formation in Beaver County, Oklahoma, at the invitation of Dr Stuart Schoff of the Geological Survey. In the marl beds they found an emydid turtle that seemed to be an unnamed species of the genus Chrysemys. Galbreath names it Chrysemys limnodytes. The holotype, museum number 7676, is part of a carapace, part of a plastron, and several marginals.
36171-told-on-the-pagoda-tales-of-burmah:
Told on the Pagoda is a set of tales of Burmah by Mimosa. Fisher Unwin of London issued the pictured tales in eighteen ninety five. Seven stories run from The Woman, The Man and The Nat onward. A fable, stolen treasure, and the vigil of Mah May follow them.

The petition to the king, the priest petition, and the king command close it. Plates show a Burmese village girl, the Mandalay palace, and a queen monastery. The Shway Dagone Pagoda stands among the pictured scenes of the land. The first tale tells of a tree spirit, or nat, who dwells therein. A woodman cut the tree unwarned, and the nat swore revenge for it.
36216-studies-in-zechariah:
A C Gaebelein wrote Studies in Zechariah, held in 1911 and shown here in its eighth edition at New York. A foreword to the eighth edition opens the book. Gaebelein says the small study was writ almost fifteen years past. Six editions had sold and a seventh was needful, he notes. He thanks God that it helped so many.

Gaebelein owns that his views have since changed on key points. He did not then tell apart the personal Antichrist and the King of the North, he says. He held the first beast of Revelation Thirteen to be the Antichrist. That view led to faults on pages one hundred and thirty five to one hundred and thirty seven, he warns. Later books give his new light, he says. Readers are asked to bear the warning in mind as they study Zechariah.
3637-the-garden-of-allah:
Robert Hichens writes a romance set in Algeria, following Domini Enfilden to the desert town of Beni-Mora. The book is built in six parts: Prelude, The Voice of Prayer, The Garden, The Journey, The Revelation, and The Journey Back. Domini arrives after a rough sea journey, unable to sleep in the Hotel de la Mer, and wakes before dawn to catch her train inland.

In the Sahara she meets a mysterious stranger and falls in love, while the desert itself becomes a test of faith and desire. Hichens writes the landscape in rich, sensual prose, with gardens, prayer, and silence shaping the story. The novel suits readers who enjoy exotic romance and a heroine seeking God and love in the same journey.
3678-jonah:
Louis Stone writes an Australian novel about Jonah, a larrikin from Cardigan Street in Sydney. The story opens with a push gathered under a veranda, smoking and discussing horses and women, all young men from eighteen to twenty. Chapters follow Jonah eating green peas, discovering a baby, dealing it out with his mates, a quiet wedding, and Jonah starting on his own.

Later chapters take Jonah to Paddy's Market, to war with rivals, to the courting of Pinkey, and to the sign of the Silver Shoe, his own boot shop. Stone writes Sydney street life with humor and warmth, following a rough hero who builds a business and a family. The novel suits readers interested in Australian urban life before the First World War.
38223-the-history-of-mendelssohn-s-orato:
F G Edwards wrote The History of Mendelssohn's Oratorio Elijah, issued by Novello in eighteen ninety-six. Sir George Grove, the great music scholar, supplies an introduction. A pencil drawing of Mendelssohn at twenty-six fronts the book. The portrait comes from Mrs Victor Benecke's keeping, the caption notes.

I have been asked to say a few words, Grove opens, in his modest way. Edwards then tells how the oratorio was born. Birmingham asked Mendelssohn for a work, and Elijah rose from the prophet's story. Letters, rehearsals, and the first performance fill his record. The oratorio became England's favourite after Handel's own. This history catches it fifty years young, with its makers still in memory.
39523-the-life-of-mohammad-the-prophet-o:
The Life of Mohammad the Prophet of Allah is a grand print life by the painter Dinet. Sliman Ben Ibrahim, an Arab, wrote the life with him in joint work. The Paris Book Club brought it out in a strict small run of print. Nine hundred plain prints and a rare set on fine stock make the run. Mohammad Racim drew the fine dress leaves that frame each part.

The book is given to the Moslem men who fell in the Great War. Dinet held that true faith folk at prayer show the Prophet path best. Stone kings of Rome stand stiff and dead by that live proof, he says. Views of Arab life and of the Hijaz, the Prophet home land, fill the plates. The first part opens with the dawn call to prayer in Mekka.
40001-an-english-girl-s-first-impression:
Beth Ellis, an English girl who went east as a visitor, wrote this travel book on Burma. It was published at Wigan and London in 1899. The front picture shows her passage through the Suez Canal, eastward ho. Her contents promise the voyage, Rangoon, and the road to Mandalay. They promise the journey to the hills, an up-country station, the European inhabitants, and the Burmese themselves, with chapters on entertaining, adventures, beasts, and sport.

The book began, she explains, at a dinner in Rangoon, where talk turned to what a newcomer sees. Pictures show elephants moving timber, bullock carts, bazaars, and a monastery. Ellis writes bright and curious, a girl's eye on an empire's outpost. The impressions are first ones, and honestly labeled so.
4246-beulah:
Augusta J. Evans set this novel in an orphan asylum, where the opening chapter finds a January sun shining on a large brick building surrounded by galleries and grounds. Beulah, the girl at its center, grows up among the asylum's inmates, under a matron's care, and the story follows her into young womanhood.

Evans, author of St. Elmo and Vashti, wrote Beulah as a novel of character and faith, in which an orphaned girl must find work, friendship, and a moral footing in the world. The long narrative moves from childhood scenes, church services, and small kindnesses toward the larger choices of adult life, with Southern settings and a strong religious thread.
43073-deutschland-u-ber-allah:
Benson wrote this wartime book, printed in London in 1917, though the catalog names no author. Its title plays on a German song and points to Germany's work in Turkey. Benson argues that Germany cared little for how France or England felt, since it meant to fight them. With Turkey, though, it took great pains to learn the mind of the people.

Benson traces how the great powers kept Turkey alive for a hundred years, each fearing a fight over its lands. He then shows how Germany used that same weak spot for its own ends in the war. The book is a sharp, one-sided look at German aims in the East, written while the war still raged.
44290-a-king-of-tyre-a-tale-of-the-times:
A King of Tyre, by James M. Ludlow, came out in New York in 1891. Ludlow calls it a tale of the times of Ezra and Nehemiah. The scene is Tyre, the isle city off the Syrian coast, in about the middle of the fifth century before Christ.

The opening paints a rich port town packed within high walls on a rock in the sea. Tall houses crowd the lanes, and two harbours swarm with ships that trade as far as Britain and Arabia. Dyers, weavers, and founders fill the shops, while the rich stroll the Great Square. One day a single topic grips all ranks alike, from state men to moulders at their doors. The tale builds its plot from that stir.
47860-the-mercy-of-allah:
The Mercy of Allah is a tale by Hilaire Belloc, printed in New York in 1922 by D. Appleton and Company. The title page gives the title in Arabic script as well as in English. The book is dedicated to Oriana Huxley Haynes. Its chapters carry Arabic names, the first called Al-Rafsat, or The Kick.

Belloc frames the work as an eastern story, told in the manner of a fable about fortune and faith. The transcriber's notes record care with the Arabic words and spellings, which shift between full and partial vowel marks in the original. The tale follows its hero through rises and falls of wealth, in the style of a parable.
49288-the-dinosaur-quarry-dinosaur-natio:
John Good, Theodore White, and Gilbert Stucker wrote a guide to the dinosaur quarry at Dinosaur National Monument in Colorado and Utah. The National Park Service issued it in Washington in 1958 at twenty five cents. A swimming apatosaur fronts the guide. The park system, the book notes, is dedicated to conserving the scenic, scientific, and historic heritage of the United States.

Contents tell of the quarry, the dinosaurs, first discoveries, and the geologic history of the bone bed. What the great reptiles looked like, their temperature tolerance, and their gizzard stones follow. The climate and landscape of Jurassic time, animals from the quarry, and why so many died there fill the mid book. Extinction and quarry history close it.
4981-minnesota-and-dacotah:
C. C. Andrews's Minnesota and Dacotah gathers letters from a tour made in the autumn before publication, more than a hundred and thirty miles northwest of St. Paul. The author set out to satisfy himself about the character and prospects of the new territory, and wrote home what he found.

The letters, dedicated to the young men of Minnesota and published in 1857, describe land, settlement, and the chances open to newcomers. Andrews writes as an observer, not a promoter, noting both promise and hardship. Readers get a firsthand snapshot of the upper Mississippi frontier just before statehood changed it forever.
50157-billie-bradley-and-the-school-myst:
Janet Wheeler wrote Billie Bradley and the School Mystery, or The Girl from Oklahoma, a girls' series book copyrighted in 1930. A picture shows Billie helpless, flinging an arm about her friend Edina. The series list shows Billie's earlier cases: an inheritance, Three Towers Hall, Lighthouse Island, Twin Lakes, and Treasure Cove among them.

The tale opens at Lake Molata, moves to a desperate fix, and brings Edina to the rescue. A battle, a public rebuke, and Billie's loyalty follow, with a tale of riches behind the mystery. Billie Bradley was the Stratemeyer syndicate's schoolgirl detective, solving mild mysteries with her chums at boarding school, in the years between the wars.
51640-a-guide-to-natural-bridges-nationa:
A Guide to Natural Bridges National Monument, Utah is a visitor guide booklet. The Canyonlands Natural History Association published the work to support the park programs of the National Park Service. The guide takes drivers along the monument road stop by stop. It opens with the twin buttes called the Bears Ears, which crown the skyline above Elk Ridge.

The text plays with the idea that a view changes with the angle of sight. It urges visitors to do more than drive in, view the three great stone bridges, and drive out. Stops along the road present rock forms such as Sphinx Rock. Plain notes explain the pale Cedar Mesa sandstone and the softer red shale layers within it. Those red beds wear away faster, and the contrast shapes the cliffs and canyons of the monument.
54854-the-yoke-of-the-thorah:
Sidney Luska wrote a novel issued by the Cassell Publishing Company in 1896. He gave the book to Edmund Clarence Stedman, whose help and praise, he says, made it live. The tale opens on the last day of November, 1882, in gray and cold.

Elias Bacharach, a young painter, finds his colors will not blend and his eye proves false. He sends his model home at two and walks out to shake off the blues. In Union Square he heads for Matthew Redwood, a costumer on Fourth Avenue, to ask how women of Provence dress for a planned work drawn from a poem by Mistral.
63787-the-purple-pariah:
The Purple Pariah is a science fiction tale by Byron Tustin, first printed in Planet Stories in March 1954. Its first lines set the tone: round and purple and sad, a being with a tale of woe. A rocket ship whirls down and crashes into a hillside. Archie Simms jumps from the hatch to the ground of an unknown world. Ed Bailey looks out after him. Fifty feet off sits the welcoming party. It is a purple sphere, eight feet across, with two huge sad eyes.

The sphere does not move when Archie shouts at it. A thrown rock misses, and the eyes watch him with yet more sorrow. Archie strokes its fur and pets it between the eyes. Ed finds their place in a guide book: the eighth planet of a far star.
66324-pariah:
Pariah is a science fiction tale by Milton Lesser, taken from Imagination for April 1954. Its blurb gives the sting at once. Harry spent three years in space waiting to get home to Earth and his family. They were waiting for him too, that is, for his corpse.

Captain Greene shakes his shaggy head at Allerton aboard the quiet ship. Allerton savours his homecoming, tapping the wallet that bulges in his tunic. He will not go out again, he says. Greene answers that none of the others are spacemen, but Allerton has the makings of one. The captain hints he will be back. The tale turns on what Earth does to men who leave it.
6869-the-american-goliah:
This pamphlet gives the only account its owners allowed of a stone figure found in Onondaga County, New York, on October 16, 1869. Shaped as a full grown man ten and one half feet tall, the figure was put forward as a petrified giant. The text gathers witness reports with the views of men of science on how such a body could turn to stone.

The publishers stress that every statement came from living witnesses on the spot, except where another source is named. They present the find as a wonder of the age and promise to add new tests, trials, and learned opinions as they arrive. The pamphlet itself serves as a running record of the Giant and its fame.
70751-archeological-investigations-in-ne:
Archeological Investigations in New Mexico, Colorado, and Utah is a report by Fewkes, issued in May 1917. It is volume sixty eight, number one, of the Smithsonian Miscellaneous Collections. The paper carries fourteen plates and is Smithsonian publication 2442 in its series. The Smithsonian Institution published it at Washington that year.

The report opens with Tebungki, or Fire House, a ruin of the Hopi country in the text. Hopi legends of clans whose ancestors peopled the Sikyatki ruin tell of that village. In their western migration they built it near a deep canyon, the legends recount in his pages. Fewkes was the dean of Southwest archaeology in his generation at the Bureau of American Ethnology. His reports join native tradition to the spade, ruin by ruin, across the plateau country of the three states in this survey.
72130-orphan-dinah:
Eden Phillpotts wrote Orphan Dinah, a novel put out in London in 1920. Phillpotts had won a name with a tale of the cash of a mean man. The tale opens on a hill top at Buckland Beacon, at the south edge of Dartmoor. 


Farm scenes at Falcon Farm and a meal at Buckland in the Moor set the world. A crash, a tor, and a house called Green Hayes mark the first third. Joe talks on the laws of trade, and a face on a rock spooks the cast. A grave rite, a sick room, and a line that the rest is easy mark the turn. Names run from Ben Bamsey and his doubts to Palk, who seeks advice. A find, the law, a nest, and a wedding day fill the close.
73527-messiah:
Gore Vidal wrote a novel of a new faith born in modern America. E P Dutton and Company issued Messiah in New York in 1954, a first form. The book is given to Tennessee Williams at the front. A quote from the Goncourt Journals of 1861 foresees a photographed god.

An old narrator owns that he was there, yet cannot trust his own memory. Eyes of memory shift from near in youth to far in age, he writes. The tale looks back on a cult that swept a nation by press and screen. Readers gain a cool, sharp fable of fame, faith, and power.
76482-the-story-of-chanukah:
Benjamin Sacks wrote this account of the festival for the Hebrew Institute of Pittsburgh, copyrighted in 1913 and dedicated to the memory of Mina Lippman Aaron. The festival, the introduction says, was set up by Judas Maccabeus and the elders of Israel on the twenty-fifth day of Kislev. The story then goes back to the death of Alexander the Great, whose kingdom split among his generals, with Egypt and Syria at war and the Jews between them.

From that strife the tale works toward the rededication of the Temple and the lights of the feast. It was written for young readers of the institute. The book is a short, clear telling of why Chanukah is kept.
76998-jonah:
Robert Nathan wrote Jonah, a short novel published at New York in 1925. Nathan had written the novels Autumn and The Puppet Master before it. The publisher was McBride and Company, and the book is dedicated to Alice and Arthur Carns.

Nathan retells the Bible story of the prophet Jonah in his own gentle prose. The opening pages picture the prophets of Israel in the desert beyond the Jordan. They live in caves and clay huts, a holy and severe company. Jonah comes out of that world of men whose ears are pierced by the voice of God. Nathan's telling is quiet and tender, far from a sermon. It gives the old tale the shape of a modern fable about a man who runs from his calling.
79101-passage-to-gomorrah:
Passage to Gomorrah is a tale of the stars by Robert Young. A front blurb calls its lead wife the most fair stray wife of the star host. A man who takes her couch in a time storm books the same dread trip, it warns. The Lady Berenice boards a small ship with one guest bunk and one fly man.

Her short gold hair puts the fly man in mind of the grain of Mars, and her wide blue eyes of ice lakes of a cold world. Her papers are passed to him by a firm man past the lift locks. Blast comes past a short span, and she must strap her self to the couch past the push. She bears a child she may not keep, and her cast out trip waits past the storm. The tale turns on that ban and on her hid love.
8016-the-bible-king-james-version-book-1:
Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, hears that Jerusalem's walls lie in ruins and asks leave to rebuild them. The book that bears his name tells how he organised the work, wall by wall and gate by gate, despite mockery, threats, and plots from neighbouring peoples. It also records his reforms: debts forgiven, Sabbath kept, and the law read aloud to a weeping crowd gathered in the square.

Nehemiah is a book about rebuilding after ruin, and its hero is an organiser as much as a prophet. His prayers alternate with practical orders, giving the story unusual energy. In the King James Version, the first-person passages feel immediate, as if Nehemiah himself were reporting. The book has long encouraged readers facing the task of starting again.
8023-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Isaiah, the longest prophetic book, spans the crisis of Judah in the eighth century BC and looks far beyond it. The prophet denounces empty worship, corrupt rulers, and trust in foreign powers, warning that Assyria will punish the nation. Then, in passages of extraordinary poetry, he promises comfort: a suffering servant who bears the people's griefs, a new Jerusalem, and a peace in which swords become ploughshares. Both judgment and hope sound in the same voice.

Isaiah's influence is immense, in Jewish liturgy, in Handel's Messiah, and in Christian reading of the servant songs. Its images, the vineyard, the highway in the desert, the light to the nations, have shaped Western imagination. In the King James Version, the book's grandeur of language matches its scope, from court intrigue to the ends of the earth.
8024-the-bible-king-james-version-book-2:
Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah of Anathoth, received God's word in the thirteenth year of King Josiah and kept prophesying through Jehoiakim and Zedekiah until Jerusalem was carried captive. His book is the longest in the Bible, mixing sermons, laments, symbolic acts, and personal confessions. He warns of Babylon's coming judgment, denounces false prophets who promise peace, and buys a field in besieged Jerusalem as a sign of future return.

Jeremiah is called the weeping prophet because his message cost him so much: prison, a cistern, and exile. Yet his promise of a new covenant, written on hearts rather than stone, became central to later faith. In the King James Version, his voice, tender and furious by turns, makes the book a profound study of a prophet who could not stay silent.
8038-the-bible-king-james-version-book-3:
Zechariah prophesied in Jerusalem in the second year of King Darius, after the exiles had returned from Babylon. His book opens with a call to turn back to God, unlike the fathers who ignored the former prophets. And then unfolds in a series of night visions: horsemen, horns, a measuring line, and a lampstand fed by olive trees. Later chapters promise a cleansed priesthood, a humble king riding on a donkey, and a restored city.

The visions are strange and vivid, and they encouraged a discouraged people to finish rebuilding the temple. Christians later read the humble king and the pierced one in these chapters as pointing to Jesus. In the King James Version, Zechariah's blend of warning and hope makes it one of the most imaginative books among the minor prophets.
8069-expositions-of-holy-scripture-isaia:
Alexander Maclaren's expositions on Isaiah, chapters one to forty-eight, and on Jeremiah work through the prophets sermon by sermon. His Isaiah titles include The Great Suit: Jehovah versus Judah, The Stupidity of Godlessness, What Sin Does to Men. The Perpetual Pillar of Cloud and Fire, A Prophet's Woes, Vision and Service, and The Kingdom and the King. Each exposition takes a passage and presses its meaning for the hearer's life.

Maclaren preaches the prophets as moral teachers, not distant oracles, and his commentary keeps the historical setting in view. The volume suits readers studying Isaiah and Jeremiah chapter by chapter, whether for preaching or private reading. It remains a respected example of Victorian expository preaching at its clearest.
8243-the-world-english-bible-web-nehemia:
Nehemiah was a Jewish official serving a Persian king when news reached him that Jerusalem lay in ruins. Its walls were broken and its gates burned, and the people who had returned from exile lived in shame and danger. With the king's leave, he traveled to Jerusalem and set about rebuilding the wall, facing mockery, threats, and plots from hostile neighbors.

The book mixes Nehemiah's own first-person account with lists of builders, gate by gate, and a public reading of the law that moved the people to tears. It is a story of grit, prayer, and practical leadership. Readers get both a vivid picture of life after exile and a portrait of a man who organized a broken city back into a community.
8250-the-world-english-bible-web-isaiah:
Isaiah, in the World English Bible, opens with the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz concerning Judah and Jerusalem, in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Hear, heavens, and listen, earth, for Yahweh has spoken: he nourished children who rebelled against him. While the ox knows its owner and the donkey its master's crib, but Israel does not know. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book moves from judgment to comfort.

The modern version keeps Isaiah's poetry direct, from the sinful nation loaded with iniquity to the promised servant and the new Jerusalem. Its plain sentences suit both study and reading aloud. For readers approaching the longest prophet, this rendering offers his grandeur without the barrier of Jacobean English.
8251-the-world-english-bible-web-jeremia:
Jeremiah was a prophet in Jerusalem during the last troubled decades of the kingdom of Judah, before Babylon destroyed the city. Called while still young, he warned kings and crowds alike that injustice, idol worship, and false confidence would end in disaster, and he was mocked, beaten, and imprisoned for it. His laments over his own people give the book its raw, personal edge.

The book mixes sermons, symbolic acts, letters to exiles, and confessions in which Jeremiah argues with God. It ends with the fall of Jerusalem, yet also promises a new covenant written on the heart. Readers meet a prophet who suffered for his message and still held that ruin was not the last word.
8260-the-world-english-bible-web-micah:
Micah, in the World English Bible, opens with the word of Yahweh that came to Micah the Morashtite in the days of Jotham. Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem. Hear, you peoples, listen, earth, and let the Lord Yahweh be witness from his holy temple, for Yahweh comes forth. Treading the high places, while mountains melt like wax before fire and valleys split like waters poured down a steep place. Lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward, the book denounces corruption and promises restoration.

The modern version keeps Micah's courtroom imagery sharp, including his famous call to do justice, love mercy, and walk humbly. For readers of the minor prophets, this rendering gives a short, powerful book in clear contemporary language, moving from judgment to a hopeful remnant.
8265-the-world-english-bible-web-zechari:
Zechariah was a prophet among the Jews who had returned from exile to a ruined Jerusalem, and his book urges them to finish rebuilding the temple. The first half is a string of night visions: horsemen patrolling the earth, a measuring line stretched over the city, a lampstand fed by olive trees, and a flying scroll. Each vision pushes the tired builders back to work.

Later chapters speak in riddles about a humble king riding a donkey, a shepherd struck down, and a day when nations gather against Jerusalem and God intervenes. Christians have long read the humble king as pointing to Jesus. For any reader, Zechariah is a strange, vivid book where hope arrives in pictures rather than plain statements.
another-world-fragments-from-the-star-ci: Benjamin Lumley writes Another World, fragments from the star city of Montalluyah, published by Samuel Tinsley in London. The book imagines a society on another star, with its own customs, morals, and government, told through a visitor's fragments. Lumley's utopia joins Victorian speculation to a tale of wonder. Strange laws and rites fill the star city out.
beulah:
Augusta J. Evans's Beulah, her 1859 breakthrough novel, follows an orphan out of the asylum into a life she means to make her own. Beulah Benton is proud and clever: taken into the stern physician Guy Hartwell's household, she grows into a teacher and writer. Her real battle is inward. Reading philosophy and German skeptics, she argues herself out of the faith she was raised in, and finds the victory cold. Evans, not yet Augusta Evans Wilson, writes the South's most famous novel of religious doubt from inside the doubter.

The book made its young author famous on the eve of the Civil War. Its dialogues on faith fill drawing rooms as other novels fill ballrooms. Readers get the nineteenth-century woman's novel of ideas here: a heroine whose mind is the plot, and whose return to belief is argued, not assumed, page by hard page.
britannica-1911-abijah:
Abijah receives a Bible entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The name, meaning Yah is father, belongs to nine men of the Old Testament. Four earn notice in the entry, drawn from Kings, Chronicles, and Samuel.

Rehoboam's son heads the list, king of Judah for about two years, with Kings and Chronicles at odds over his tale. Samuel's second son follows, a judge at Beersheba whose misconduct fed Israel's demand for a king. Jeroboam's young son, dead early, comes third. Last stands the head of the eighth priestly order, the order of Zacharias, father of John the Baptist. The form Abijam is likely a copy error, the entry closes.
britannica-1911-ahaziah:
Two kings share the name Ahaziah, a name that means Yahweh sustains, and both met bad ends. The first ruled Israel as its eighth king, the son and heir of Ahab, for less than two years. As soon as he took the throne, the Moabites ceased to pay the tribute they had owed Israel.

A fall from a lattice in an upper room of his palace left Israel's Ahaziah sick in bed. He sent men to ask the oracle of Baal-zebub at Ekron about his fate, but Elijah met the party and sent back word that the king was sure to die. Judah's Ahaziah, its sixth king, had Jehoram for his father and Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, for his mother. He ruled one year, stands in the record as wicked and given to idol worship, and was slain by Jehu. Men also call him Jehoahaz and Azariah.
britannica-1911-ahmad-shah:
Ahmad Shah (1724–1773) founded the Durani line in Afghanistan after a youth spent as a captive. He was the son of Sammaun-Khan, the born chief of the Abdali tribe. As a boy he fell into the hands of the foe tribe of Ghilzais, who kept him prisoner at Kandahar. Nadir Shah freed him in 1738 and soon set him over a body of Abdali horse.

Nadir was slain in 1747. Ahmad tried and failed to grab the Persian treasure, then drew back to Afghanistan. The tribes there took him as their ruler, and he was crowned at Kandahar that October, giving his tribe the new name Durani. He held power two ways: by leaving each tribe largely free, asking only its fair share of tribute and service, and by keeping his troops busy abroad. His fall on Delhi in 1756 left the city looted for more than a month.
britannica-1911-allah: Muslims of every nation call the one true God Allah, an Arabic name built from al, the article, joined to ilah, a god. Kindred forms show up in Hebrew and Aramaic, and in old Arabic from Sabaean inscriptions. Where the root itself comes from stays very doubtful; Lane's Arabic-English Lexicon and the Oxford Hebrew lexicon are named for the rival evidence.
britannica-1911-athaliah:
Athaliah, a queen named in the Bible, is the subject of a brief 1911 Britannica article. She was the daughter of Ahab and the wife of Jehoram, king of Judah. After the death of her son Ahaziah, she seized the throne. She then ruled for six years.

She is said to have killed all the royal house of Judah. One child, Joash, was hid in the temple by his aunt, the wife of the priest Jehoida. That priest led a revolt in favor of Joash. Athaliah and her backers were put to death. The piece notes that her tale forms the base of a famed play by Racine. Handel and Mendelssohn also set it to music.
britannica-1911-ayah: Ayah, from the Spanish word aya, is a children's nurse or maid. Portuguese speakers carried the word into India, and the English there took it up for their native nurses. The very short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces that path, from Spanish homes through Portuguese India into English use, in two lines.
britannica-1911-azariah:
Azariah is the name of several men in the Old Testament, and the entry sorts fourteen of them in order. Two served King Solomon's court: a son of Zadok the priest among his princes, and a son of Nathan as a high official. Others include a prophet under King Asa and captains made officers by Jehoiada the priest.

Kings carry the name too: a king of Judah, son of Amaziah, also called Uzziah, and another also called Ahaziah and Jehoahaz. One Azariah restored Nehemiah's wall at Jerusalem under Artaxerxes' commission; another opposed the prophet Jeremiah. The last named is Daniel's companion, renamed Abednego by Nebuchadrezzar and cast with two friends into the fiery furnace for refusing to worship the golden image.
britannica-1911-bander-lingah:
Bander Lingah, or Linga, is a town of Persia on the northern shore of the Persian Gulf, about 300 miles by sea from Bushire. Its population was about 10,000. Like Bander Abbasi, it belongs to the Persian Gulf ports division, whose governor resides at Bushire.

Trade through the port ran high: exports and imports averaged about £800,000 a year in 1890–1905, though nearly half of that was pearls in transit from the Arab coast fisheries to Bombay. The 1911 Britannica entry notes the port serves the province of Laristan, with a British post office and weekly steamers. For generations an Arab sheikh's tribe held the place, until a Persian force expelled the Arabs in 1898.
britannica-1911-berlin-isaiah: Isaiah Berlin (1725–1799), a rabbi of Breslau, is covered in a single-sentence entry in the 1911 Britannica. The entry calls him eminent and credits him with sharp, acute notes on the Talmud. Those notes, it states, had a real influence in moving the critical study of the Talmud forward. No works are listed by title, and no details of his life beyond his Breslau post and his dates are given.
britannica-1911-bernhardt-sarah:
Sarah Bernhardt (1845– ), born Rosine Bernard in Paris, was a French actress of mixed French and Dutch parentage. She was baptized at twelve and raised in a convent. At thirteen she entered the Conservatoire. She won second prizes there for tragedy and comedy. Her debut at the Comédie Française came in 1862. It brought no marked success at first.

The 1911 Britannica entry traces her real rise at the Odéon theatre. Cordelia, the queen in Ruy Blas, and Zanetto in Le Passant made her name. She then returned to the Comédie Française. Phèdre in 1874 and Dona Sol in Hernani in 1877 confirmed her standing. Later she played Hamlet in Paris and London, and Napoleon's son in L'Aiglon.
britannica-1911-bertinoro-obadiah:
Obadiah of Bertinoro was a Jewish commentator on the Mishnah who died in Jerusalem about 1500. This short 1911 Britannica entry credits him with much improving the state of Jews in the Holy Land. Before he migrated there, it says, the Jews of Palestine lived in poverty and persecution. His own move east frames the brief life story told here. No birth date or birth place is given.

His commentary on the Mishnah is called the most useful of all helps to understanding that work. It is printed in most Hebrew editions of the Mishnah. Surenhusius translated the commentary into Latin for his Amsterdam edition of 1698 to 1703. That wide printing explains Bertinoro's lasting place in study of the Mishnah. The entry is only a few lines long.
britannica-1911-bigsby-john-jeremiah:
John Jeremiah Bigsby (1792–1881) was an English geologist and physician, born at Nottingham. He took his medical degree at Edinburgh. In 1817 he joined the army medical service at the Cape of Good Hope. A year later he went to Canada as a regimental medical officer. Geology caught his interest there. In 1819 he was commissioned to report on the geology of Upper Canada.

He served as British secretary to the Boundary Commission from 1822, the 1911 Britannica entry says. His Canadian researches filled papers and his 1850 book The Shoe and Canoe. Back in England he practised medicine, then settled in London in 1846. His last twenty years went to fossil lists of Palaeozoic rocks. His Thesaurus Siluricus appeared in 1868 and its Devonian sequel in 1878. He founded the Bigsby medal in 1877.
britannica-1911-buxton-jedediah:
Jedediah Buxton, an English man of numbers born in seventeen hundred and seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Elmton near Chesterfield, he was the son of the parish school man. His grand sire had been the priest of the same parish. Yet his own school years were so lost that he could not write at all.

Past the world of numbers his store of facts was most thin. How he first came to grasp the ties of numbers, he could not tell in his own tale. His mind sat on numbers with no break. He oft took no note of the things round him save as they bore a count. He paced off a whole lord tract of a thousand acres on foot.
britannica-1911-calah:
Calah was an old city of Assyria and one of its capitals, as a 1911 Britannica entry records. It stood where the Tigris meets the upper Zab, south of Nineveh. Stone texts say Shalmaneser the First built it about 1300 before Christ as a royal seat. After a fall into ruin it was rebuilt by Assur nasir pal about 880.

From then on it stayed a seat of Assyrian kings until the realm fell. Medes and Babylonians took and wrecked it late in the seventh century. Layard found the site in 1845 in the mound of Nimrud. Hebrew tale in Genesis links its building to Nimrod, and local lore does the same.
britannica-1911-cowley-hannah:
Hannah Cowley (1743–1809) was an English dramatist and poet, daughter of a bookseller at Tiverton in Devonshire. At about twenty-five she wed a man of the East India Company's service. He died in 1797. Some years after her marriage she sat at the theatre with her husband one night. She told him she could write as good a piece as the one on stage.

Within a fortnight she had written her first play, The Runaway, to prove the claim. She sent it to Garrick, who staged it at Drury Lane in 1776. Between then and 1795 she wrote twelve more plays. All but one of them played at Drury Lane or Covent Garden. The Belle's Stratagem, from 1782, still holds a place on the stage. Her poems, mainly on past events, draw less praise in the entry. As Anna Matilda she held a verse duel in print that made the name a byword.
britannica-1911-cuddapah:
Cuddapah is a town and district of British India in the Madras Presidency. The town stands six miles from the right bank of the river Pennar and 161 miles by rail from Madras. Its population in 1901 was 16,432, and the entry calls it now a poor place. Hills close it on three sides, and it bears a bad name for health. Cotton and indigo trade, with cotton cloth making, sustain it.

The district covers 8,723 square miles, split by the Eastern Ghats into a low plain and a high table-land. The Pennar crosses it eastwards, shrinking to a small stream in the hot months. Its noted antiquity is the fort of Gurramkonda, guarded in legend by a horse whose theft broke the spell of its strength. The district held 1,291,267 people in 1901. Millet, rice, cotton, and indigo lead its crops, and steam presses handle the cotton.
britannica-1911-dahabeah:
Dahabeah is an Arabic word for a native passenger boat used on the Nile, says a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. The word is spelt in many ways, and two roots are offered for it. One is the word for gold, and one a verb form that means to go. The typical boat is a barge like house boat fitted with sails.

Its shape recalls the painted galleys shown on the tombs of the Pharaohs. State barges of like kind were used by the Muslim rulers of Egypt. Their gilding may account for the gold derivation. Before steamers came, travellers going up the Nile used such boats as a rule. They are still favoured by the leisured and wealthy classes. Modern boats are often made of iron and hold from two to a dozen passengers.
britannica-1911-elijah:
Elijah, whose Hebrew name means Yahweh is God, stands as the sternest of the Hebrew prophets. A 1911 Britannica entry marks how he bursts into the Bible tale with no soft lead in. His main work fell in the reign of Ahab in the ninth century before Christ. He foretold a drought sent as punishment for apostasy led by Queen Jezebel.

By the brook Cherith he hid from wrath and drank from the stream in safety. Ravens brought him bread and flesh each morning and night in that retreat. When the brook dried up, the prophet moved on at the word of God. The entry weighs even the place of that brook with close care.
britannica-1911-etah:
Etah is a town and district of British India in the Agra division of the United Provinces. The town stands on the Grand Trunk road and had 8,796 people in 1901. The district covers 1,737 square miles of alluvial plateau above the Ganges valley. The Ganges canal waters the uplands. A belt of rich silt land lies between the river's modern and ancient beds. The Kali Nadi stream drains the centre through a deep gorge.

The district held an early Aryan settlement, and the pilgrim Hsüan Tsang noted its temples and monasteries in the 7th century. Rajputs later took it from aboriginal tribes. It passed under Mahmud of Ghazni in 1017 and came to the British in 1801 under the treaty of Lucknow. Serious disturbances marked the mutiny of 1857. The 1901 population was 863,948, up 23 per cent in the decade as canal irrigation spread.
britannica-1911-etawah:
Etawah is a town and district of British India in the Agra division of the United Provinces. The town stands on the left bank of the Jumna, 206 miles from Allahabad by rail. Its 1901 population was 42,570. Deep fissures cut through its quarters, crossed by bridged roads. The Jama Masjid, first a Hindu temple, is its chief ornament. Trade runs by rail and river, and manufactures include cotton cloth, combs and horn-ware.

The district covers 1,691 square miles across the Doab plain and beyond the Jumna to the Chambal gorges. The north-east is rich, watered by branches of the Ganges canal. The south-west lacks large irrigation works and is less fruitful. Ravines near the Jumna shelter scattered herdsmen. During the mutiny of 1857 rebels held the district from June to December. Its 1901 population was 806,798, up 11 per cent in the decade.
britannica-1911-fenton-elijah:
Elijah Fenton was an English poet who lived from sixteen eighty three to seventeen thirty. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Shelton near Newcastle under Lyme, of an old Staffordshire family. He took his degree from Jesus College, Cambridge, in seventeen o four.

Faith scruples kept Fenton from taking church orders after his studies there. He went to Flanders as secretary to the earl of Orrery for a time. He taught school at Headley, then led the free school at Sevenoaks. Hope of a post from Bolingbroke failed, and he tutored Lord Broghill instead. He is best recalled as Pope aide on the Odyssey rendering work.
britannica-1911-grew-nehemiah:
Nehemiah Grew (1641-1712) was an English vegetable anatomist and physiologist, son of the Nonconformist divine Obadiah Grew, born in Warwickshire in 1641. The 1911 Britannica entry has him graduating at Cambridge in 1661 and taking his M.D. at Leiden ten years later. He began observing the anatomy of plants in 1664.

His essay The Anatomy of Vegetables begun reached the Royal Society in 1670, and he was elected a fellow the next year. Settling in London in 1672, he built an extensive medical practice. In 1677 he succeeded Oldenburg as the Society's secretary and edited the Philosophical Transactions. His catalogue of the rarities at Gresham College appeared in 1681. His great Anatomy of Plants followed in 1682, in four books. The entry presents him as a founder of the science of plant structure.
britannica-1911-hamah:
Hamah is the Hamath of the Bible. It was a Hittite royal city in Syria. It sits in the narrow valley of the Orontes. Damascus lies 110 miles to the south. The river winds past and four bridges span it. Houses rise 150 feet above the water on the south-east. Twenty-four minarets rise from its mosques. Its population is about 40,000. Huge water-wheels lifting Orontes water are its famous sight.

Shalmaneser II of Assyria took Hamath in 854 BC. He slew 14,000 allied troops at Karkor. Tiglath Pileser made it tributary in 738 BC. Sargon crushed another rebellion in 720 BC. Greeks renamed it Epiphania after Antiochus Epiphanes. It surrendered to Omar's general in AD 639. Tancred captured it in 1108 and massacred its defenders. Saladin occupied it in 1178. Its bazaars trade considerably with the Bedouins.
britannica-1911-hezekiah:
Hezekiah, whose name means my strength is of Yah, was a son of Ahaz and one of the greatest kings of Judah. He flourished at the end of the 8th and start of the 7th century B.C. Much in his reign is unsure, apart from the great crisis of 701 B.C. Even whether he took the throne before or after Samaria fell in 722–721 B.C. is disputed.

Sennacherib came to the Assyrian throne in 705, and vassal kings plotted for freedom. Judah was in league with Ekron and held its king Padi prisoner. Sennacherib routed the allies at Eltekeh and turned on Judah. The Assyrian record claims 46 towns taken and 200,150 people carried off, with Jerusalem closely besieged. Hezekiah sent a rich tribute to Nineveh, gold, silver and ivory among it. The record breaks off there, for Babylonia had revolted in 700.
britannica-1911-howrah:
Howrah is a city and district of British India, in the Burdwan division of Bengal. The city stands opposite Calcutta, joined to it by a floating bridge. Its municipal area is about 11 square miles, and its people numbered 157,594 in 1901, up 35 per cent in the decade. Since 1872 the population has almost doubled, thanks to great industrial growth. The article sits inside a chunk whose opening pages finish the Howitt article.

Howrah is the terminus of the East Indian railway, and of the Bengal-Nagpur and East Coast lines, with light railways to Amta and Sheakhala. It is the headquarters of the jute industry, with steam mills and presses, cotton and oil mills, rope-works and iron-works. Sibpur Engineering College stands on the town's edge, and many Calcutta business men live there. Its district runs south down the right bank of the Hugli to the Damodar, 510 square miles with 850,514 people in 1901.
britannica-1911-impey-sir-elijah: Sir Elijah Impey's 1911 Britannica entry survives here only as its closing lines, not as a full article. The hosted text holds a quoted judgment that he acted with absolute fairness and with as much indulgence as his duty allowed, followed by a short list of sources. Those sources are E. B. Impey's Sir Elijah Impey, dated 1846, and Sir James Stephen's The Story of Nuncomar and the Impeachment of Sir Elijah Impey, dated 1885. Nothing of the entry's own account of his life or trial is present in the file.
britannica-1911-jephthah:
Jephthah is one of the judges of Israel in the Bible, a son born out of wedlock to a man of Gilead. Cast out of his fathers house by his true born brothers, he fled to a land in Syria. There he drew round him a strong band of men with no home, like himself.

When a foe pressed his kin hard, the elders of Gilead called him home to lead them. He took the task on one term: if he won, he would be made their head. His name is best known for his rash vow, the 1911 Britannica entry says. On his glad return from war, that vow led to the death of his own daughter as a gift to God. The piece weighs why men have balked at the plain sense of the tale.
britannica-1911-josiah:
Josiah, a king of Judah in the Bible, is treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the grandson of Manasseh and came to the throne at age eight. His father Amon had been murdered, and no record tells of his boyhood years. Scythian raids of that age are not named in his tale. The fall of Assyrian power left the land in a rare spell of peace.

With Assyria weak and Babylon not yet on the march, Josiah may have hoped to build a free state of his own. Samaria lay within his reach in those years. Why he chose to bar the path of King Necho of Egypt is not clear from the text. That stand led him to the field of Megiddo, where his reign met its end. His deep reform of worship in Judah is the backdrop to the whole account.
britannica-1911-judah:
Judah was a district of ancient Palestine, south of the kingdom of Israel, set between the Dead Sea and the Philistine plain. In form it falls into three parts. The hill country runs from Hebron north through Jerusalem, the lowland, or Shephelah, lies in the west, and the dry steppe of the Negeb fills the south.

The land is one of sharp contrasts. A high, stony table land in the centre rises to 3300 feet just north of Hebron. Barren tracts lie east by the Dead Sea and in the south, though the soil near Hebron is rich. On the whole the district suited herding more than tillage. The entry traces its tangled record: rivalry with Israel under the old kings, the falls of Samaria in 722 B.C. and Jerusalem in 586 B.C., and the later breach with the Samaritans. The name of the Jews itself derives from Judah.
britannica-1911-jung-bahadur-sir-maharaj:
Sir Jung Bahadur (1816–1877) was prime minister of Nepal and grand nephew of Bhim Sena Thapa, the strong military minister who had ruled the state in fact for decades. When that supremacy was threatened, Jung Bahadur went into exile in 1838 and so escaped the fate that struck his great uncle the next year.

The leaders who took power were murdered in turn in 1843, and his uncle Matabar Singh became prime minister, making him general and chief judge. The uncle was soon put to death himself. In 1846 a quarrel was worked up in which Fateh Jung and thirty two other chiefs were killed, and the rani made Jung Bahadur sole minister. Her plot against him failed, the raja and rani fled to India, and he stood firm. He visited England from January 1850 to February 1851, reformed the penal code, and took up a war with Tibet.
britannica-1911-kermanshah:
Kermanshah is a province of Persia, lying west of Hamadan, north of Luristan, and south of Kurdistan, and reaching westward to the Turkish frontier. Its people number about 400,000, and it pays a yearly revenue of over £20,000. Many of its people are nomadic Kurds and Lurs who pay little tax.

The plains are well watered and very fertile, while the hills carry rich pastures that feed large flocks of sheep and goats. Those sheep give a great part of the meat eaten at Teheran. The province also grows much wheat and barley, and could send out great quantities for export if the means of carriage were better. Its capital, Kermanshah, stands at 5100 feet, about 220 miles from Bagdad and 250 miles from Teheran. Though ringed by fortifications with five gates and three miles in circuit, the town's strength lies in trade more than in arms.
britannica-1911-kotah:
Kotah is a native state of India in the Rajputana agency, covering 5684 square miles. The land slopes gently north from the high table-land of Malwa and is drained by the Chambal and its branches, all flowing north or north-east. The Mokandarra range runs across it, and its pass is remembered for Colonel Monson's hard retreat in 1804. Farmers grow the usual Indian grains, with wheat, cotton, poppy and a little good tobacco.

Kotah began as an offshoot of Bundi state, granted to a younger son of the Bundi raja by the emperor Shah Jahan. In 1901 the state held 544,879 people, a fall of 24 per cent after famine. Its revenue is put at £206,000, with tribute of £28,000. Opium and grain are the chief exports. The town of Kotah stands on the right bank of the Chambal, walled and split into three parts, and held 33,679 people in 1901.
britannica-1911-kumishah:
Kumishah is a district and town in the province of Isfahan, Persia. The hosted text for this record is a segment inside a shared file that also holds neighbouring entries; the passage described here is the town's own article. The district runs 50 miles long and 16 miles broad, holds about 40 villages, and grows much grain. The town stands on the high road from Isfahan to Shiraz, 52 miles S. of Isfahan.

Kumishah was once a flourishing city, several miles round, until the Afghans destroyed it in 1722. It is now a decayed place, with crumbling walls and falling towers and barely 15,000 people. South of the town runs a level plain as far as the village Maksudbeggi, 16 miles away. On that plain, on the 28th of February 1835, an army of Mahommed Shah, 2000 men with 16 guns under Sir H. Lindsay-Bethune, routed the 6000 men of the shah's two rebellious uncles.
britannica-1911-kutaiah: Kutaiah, also written Kutaya or Kiutahia, is the chief town of a sanjak in the vilayet of Brusa, in Asia Minor. It stands on the Pursaksu, a branch of the Sakaria, the ancient Sangarius, at a key point of the great road across Asia Minor from Constantinople to Aleppo. A branch line links it with the Anatolian railway. It carries on a busy trade, its people are put at about 22,000, and it has been identified with the ancient Cotiaeum.
britannica-1911-markland-jeremiah: Jeremiah Markland, an English scholar of the classics who lived from 1693 to 1776, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Childwall in Lancashire and schooled at Christ's Hospital and Peterhouse, Cambridge. He died at Milton, near Dorking, in July 1776. His key works include a critical letter of 1723 and an edition of the Sylvae of Statius in 1728. He also wrote notes on Lysias, Maximus of Tyre, and plays of Euripides, and remarks on the letters of Cicero to Brutus.
britannica-1911-mason-sir-josiah:
Sir Josiah Mason (1795-1881) was an English maker of steel pens, born in Kidderminster. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows his rise from street hawking of cakes and fruit. He tried many trades before settling in Birmingham in 1814. Split rings by machine came first, then steel pens in volume.

His pens sold under a London stationer name, which hid his scale. He was in fact the largest pen maker in England, it says. Other ventures covered plating, copper work, and rubber rings as well. Self taught and keenly aware of gaps in his schooling, he gave vast sums to learning. His orphanage and college gifts ran to hundreds of thousands of pounds.
britannica-1911-more-hannah:
Hannah More, a writer of three careers, is followed in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Bristol in 1745, she was a schoolmaster's daughter. Her elder sisters ran a boarding school in Bristol town. Hannah learned there from the age of twelve with the girls. Her first works were small plays in verse for young ladies.

In time she made a name as a wit in high company. Johnson, Reynolds, and Garrick all knew her in that bright circle. A broken engagement left her free, with a yearly sum to live on. London then drew her for a life of letters in full. Sacred Dramas of 1782 ran through nineteen printings in its day. Later she turned to moral prose and acts of good works.
britannica-1911-mullah:
Mullah is a title used in Muslim lands for a man of learning. The 1911 Britannica entry traces the word to an Arabic term, maula. That word first marked the bond between a freed slave and his old master. In India the title fits the man who reads the Koran aloud. It also fits a Muslim school master who teaches the young.

In some lands the sway of mullahs is vast in scope. In Afghanistan their voice with the crowd can rival the amir's own. On the north west frontier of India they near lead whole tribes. The entry cites the risings of 1897 and 1898 as proof. A famed mad mullah of Swat led one such attack in person.
britannica-1911-paducah:
Paducah, a city in Kentucky in the United States, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the seat of McCracken county, at the point where the Tennessee river joins the Ohio. It lies about 50 miles east of Cairo in Illinois. Its count rose from 12,707 in 1890 to 19,446 in 1900 and 22,760 in 1910.

Paducah sits in a rich farming region and does a large wholesale trade. Goods traded there are food stores, whisky, tobacco, hardware, grain, and live stock. It is a great market for loose leaf tobacco and a base for tow boats that carry coal down the Mississippi. Rail lines meet there and keep large repair shops in the city. Steam boats link it to river ports such as Louisville, Saint Louis, and New Orleans.
britannica-1911-pujah: Pujah is a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the Hindu rites used in the worship of idols. The entry adds that British users in India had stretched the word to mean any rite at all. Their stock example was the pujah of the flag, the sepoy term for the trooping of the colours.
britannica-1911-rayah:
Rayah is the name given to the non Moslem subjects of a Moslem ruler, as the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains. The Arabic word means peasants, subjects, flock, or herd in its senses. All who pay the haraj, or poll tax levied on unbelievers, count as rayahs by that rule. Five classes of rayahs existed under Turkish rule in the empire.

Those classes were the Greek, the Armenian, and the Catholic Armenian communities in order. The Latin Christians and the Jews made up the fourth and fifth classes. The name rayah is most commonly used of the peasants in speech. It does not apply only to the agricultural populations of the land, the text stresses. Status as a rayah depended on religious faith, not on the work a man did for his bread.
britannica-1911-rotumah:
Rotumah is an island of the South Pacific Ocean, a dependency of Fiji. Its island entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies about three hundred miles north of Fiji, ringed by coral reefs. Rich woods cover the isle, whose highest ground reaches eight hundred feet.

About twenty two hundred people live on Rotumah and near small isles. The natives are Polynesian, though their tongue is classed as Melanesian here. Most follow the Wesleyan faith or the Roman Catholic faith today. Copra is the chief product that the island sends out for trade. A board of a commissioner, chiefs, and magistrates makes local laws there.
britannica-1911-shekinah:
Shekinah is a Hebrew word that means that which dwells, or the dwelling. A 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry traces its use in the Targums. Those are the Aramaic versions of Bible readings used in the synagogue.

Scribes took great care with words that made God seem like a man. They used round about phrases and broad terms to guard the sense. Where the Hebrew text spoke of God in a place, they put Shekinah in its place. One case cited is the verse that says God will dwell among the children of Israel. The Targum form says God will cause his Shekinah to dwell in their midst. So the word came to stand for God himself.
britannica-1911-shenandoah:
Shenandoah is a borough of Schuylkill county, Pennsylvania, described in this 1911 Britannica article. It lies about forty miles north-north-west of Reading, and its people numbered 25,774 in the census of 1910. Among the foreign-born, Lithuanians and Poles stood first, and both peoples had newspapers printed in the town.

Three railways served the borough, which had a public library. Its Greek Catholic church, set up as St Michael's Parish in 1885, is said to be the first of that body in the United States. Shenandoah sits in the great anthracite coal region of Pennsylvania, and mining and shipping coal were its chief trades. A log house stood on the site as early as 1835, but growth waited until the first colliery opened in 1862, and the borough was made in 1866.
britannica-1911-siddons-sarah:
Sarah Siddons (1755–1831) was an English actress, the eldest of twelve children of Roger Kemble. She was born in a public house at Brecon in Wales on 5 July 1755. Her mother took care to send her to schools in the towns where the troupe played. So, though she acted on the stage as a child, she gained a fine schooling. She grew close to William Siddons, an actor of the troupe, but her parents were against the match.

Her parents wished her to take a squire who had asked for her hand. Siddons was sent from the troupe, and she was placed as a lady's maid at Guy's Cliff in Warwickshire. There she read Shakespeare, Milton, and Rowe aloud in the hall of the staff. At times she read before the gentry of the house as well.
britannica-1911-tattnall-josiah:
Josiah Tattnall was an American sea chief who lived from seventeen ninety-five to eighteen seventy-one. He was born near Savannah and schooled in England. He joined the sea force in eighteen twelve and served till the Civil War. His world fame came from one bold act in China.

There he used the line that blood is more thick than water to back his choice. He brought his ship in range and lent boats to aid a British fleet in a failed storm of forts. In the Civil War he led the sea force of the South. Its means were too thin for more than river fights.
britannica-1911-webster-noah:
Noah Webster, who lived from 1758 to 1843, was an American maker of word books and a journalist. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at West Hartford, Connecticut, on the sixteenth of October 1758. He came of old Hartford stock on both sides. He entered Yale in 1774 and took his degree in 1778. He read law and joined the bar in 1781. A spell of school teaching showed him the want of good English school books.

From 1783 Webster put out his Grammatical Institute in three parts: a speller, a grammar, and a reader. It was the first American work of its kind. The speller sold over a million copies a year before 1861, on a fee of less than a cent each. Its wide use made American speech more even across the land. It also spread the plain spelling that marks American English.
britannica-1911-wedgwood-josiah:
Josiah Wedgwood, the most distinguished of English makers of pottery, who lived from 1730 to 1795, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He came of a family long established as potters in Staffordshire through the 1600s. Josiah, born in 1730, was the youngest child of a potter of Burslem.

His father owned a small but thriving pottery in Burslem at his birth. At a very early age Josiah distinguished himself by keen powers of observation and interest in all that was curious and beautiful. Soon after the death of his father in 1739, the boy, scarcely ten years of age, was taken from school. He was set to learn the art of throwing clay, shaping vessels on the wheel. At that art he soon became extraordinarily skilful in his work. In 1744 he was apprenticed to his eldest brother, who had succeeded to the pottery.
britannica-1911-wells-charles-jeremiah:
Charles Jeremiah Wells, an English poet who lived from about 1798 to 1879, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in London, most likely in 1798. He was schooled at Edmonton, at the school of Cowden Clarke. Among his schoolmates was Tom Keats, the younger brother of the poet.

Wells came to know John Keats himself. He was the friend who sent Keats roses. Keats wrote a sonnet to him in June 1816, on the gift. The poem speaks of peace, truth, and friendliness in the scent. Soon after, Wells played a cruel practical joke on the dying Tom Keats. In the elder poet's letters he then appears as that degraded Wells. The piece opens with a friendship sung in verse, then soured for good. Poetry readers meet a minor poet kept in view by a great one's lines.
britannica-1911-zephaniah:
Zephaniah is a Bible study in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the ninth of the minor prophets. His name means that Yahweh hides or stores up. The text traces his line through his great grandfather Hezekiah. That man may have been the well known king of Judah.

The article places his work in the time of King Josiah. His fifty three verses warn Judah and Jerusalem of doom. They also hold out a calm time to come. Woven through both is the thought of a world wide judgment. That judgment would leave Yahweh as lord of all the earth. The piece then works through the book part by part. It weighs hard points of date, of heathen rites, and of the Day of Yahweh.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-allah:
Allah, the name of God in Arabic, compounds al and ilah, divinity, signifying the god par excellence. The form itself proves ilah was once an appellative, common to local and tribal gods. With the article it came to be restricted to one god who took precedence, and finally, with monotheism's triumph, was recognized as the only true God. The same root occurs in all Semitic languages for the Divinity.

Whether the name began as a proper name pointing to an early monotheism, later deviating into polytheism, is debated. It may instead have been an appellative that became a proper name only at monotheism. Before Mohammed's time the Arabs, through contact with Jews and Christians, were monotheists. Allah in Arabic theology matches God among Jews and Christians, except for the Trinity, which the Koran excludes. His attributes, denied by the Motazilites, number ninety-nine, each a bead of the Moslem chaplet.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-amrah:
In central Syria, where wood was scarce and the land often overrun by armies and brigands, builders learned to raise houses of stone alone. One such house at Amrah survives in fine condition. It stands round three sides of a courtyard, with a great hall rising two stories high. Its ground-floor bedrooms hold small canopied alcoves, and cupboards are cut from the thickness of the stone walls.

Houses of this Hauran kind sheltered the upper and middle classes from the third century to the seventh. Their stone craft explains why so many still stand. The Amrah house found a new life in modern times as the home of the sheikh of Douma. His household lives upstairs while business runs below, and the great hall keeps its ancient uses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bettiah:
Bettiah, a Prefecture Apostolic in northern India, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Its jurisdiction includes the whole native state of Nepal, over 59,000 square miles with nearly three million people, bounded by Tibet, the Ghagra, the Ganges, and the Kusi. Capuchin missions opened the field.

In 1738 Father Joseph of Carignano, travelling toward Nepal and Tibet, stopped at Bettiah and cured the town's queen, who in return allowed him to preach. The Nepal war of 1769 and later troubles broke the mission's growth, but stations and schools survived. The entry is a frontier mission report on India's northern edge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-book-of-nehem:
The Book of Nehemiah, also called the second Book of Esdras, tells how Jerusalem's walls rose again under Persian rule. Talmud and early Church counted it one book with Esdras, and Jerome still treated them together. Both were compiled and edited together, probably by the author of Paralipomenon about 300 before Christ. Nehemiah's own memoirs, however, justify reading it apart.

Its three sections open with Nehemiah, cup-bearer to Artaxerxes at Susa, hearing of Jerusalem's ruin in the king's twentieth year. His prudence wins him a mission with full powers to rebuild, lasting twelve years under the title Perah, or Athersatha. Earlier Jewish attempts under Xerxes and Artaxerxes I had stalled, and enemies had torn down part of the work. The middle section raises special literary problems and is treated last, after the wall narrative and the final chapter.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-delilah:
A scriptural entry examines Delilah, the woman of the valley of Sorek whom Samson loved after his exploit at Gaza. Sorek, known to Eusebius and Jerome and placed north of Eleutheropolis near Samson's home, is now Khan Sureq, on the borderland between Israelites and Philistines. Though Scripture never states her people, her dealings with Philistine princes make it unlikely she was an Israelite.

Nor is it likely she was Samson's wife: the text's phrasing, the Philistines' easy access to her house, and her readiness to betray him suggest a harlot, the common view among commentators. Believing Samson's strength came from a magical charm, the princes paid her to learn its secret. After false answers and mock bindings, her importunity won the truth: his Nazarite consecration and uncut hair. She had it shorn as he slept and handed him to his enemies.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-elijah:
Elijah, called Elias in this entry, was the loftiest prophet of the Old Testament, known chiefly from the narratives in the First Book of Kings. His Hebrew name means Yahveh is God. The stories, likely shaped in northern Israel near his own time, paint him in graphic detail. He is a desert man in a skin garment and leather girdle. He is swift of foot, at home in torrent beds and mountain caves.

He bursts onto the scene to tell King Ahab that God will punish Israel's apostasy with a long drought. Ahab, pushed by his Tyrian wife Jezebel, had built a Baal temple at Samaria, brought in foreign priests, and persecuted Yahveh's prophets. Of Elijah's birthplace nothing is sure, save that he was a Tishbite. The entry calls him a fire whose word burned like a torch. It follows his sudden comings and goings with the king.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jonah:
Jonah is the fifth of the Minor Prophets, hero of the book that bears his name. His name usually means dove, but Jerome derived it from a root meaning to mourn, fitting his complaining words in chapter four. Outside his book he appears in 2 Kings, where Jeroboam II's recovery of Israel's borders fulfills the word spoken by Jonah son of Amittai of Gath-Hepher. Gath-Hepher was his probable birthplace, where his grave was shown in Jerome's day.

A tradition made him the son of the widow of Zarephath revived by Elijah, but the entry finds no basis for it beyond a play on names. The book's interest lies in two incidents: God's command to preach to Nineveh, Jonah's flight toward Tarshish, the storm, his confession, and his casting into the sea. They were followed by his reluctant preaching and Nineveh's repentance, which left the prophet complaining at God's mercy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-machpelah:
Machpelah is the burial ground by ancient Hebron that Abraham purchased from Ephron the Hittite for Sarah's grave. Sarah, Abraham, Rebecca, Leah, and lastly Jacob all rest in its cave, as Genesis records.

Hebrew usage, always with the article, makes Machpelah the field holding the cave, while Greek renders it the double cave, from kafal, to double, a sense taken into Targum, Syriac, and Vulgate. Josephus knows the tomb in the Hebron district. Rabbinic lore adds four patriarchs and even Adam, and Jerome carried that reading into the Vulgate. The Haram in south-east Hebron is identified with the tomb Josephus describes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-massorah:
Massorah is the textual tradition of the Hebrew Bible, an official record of its words, consonants, vowels, and accents. The word may come from a verb meaning to hand down, seen in Ezekiel 20:37, or from a verb meaning to bind, since in the Mishna it chiefly means tradition. The main evidence for Massorah is the text itself in Hebrew Bible manuscripts, plus collections and marginal notes.

Jews treated sacred books as inspired code and record for national unity, so copyists from the first century B.C. trained to fix the text exactly, shunning novelty. Hebrew had no vowel letters, so certain consonants, matres lectionis, marked long vowels, and Sopherim, counters, counted every Torah letter. Later marginal notes marked Qere, read but not written, and Kethibh, written but not read.
