Seventeenth-century Protestants like the Buxtorfs called the text infallible, but modern critics treat it as one second-century witness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-messiah:
Messiah, the Greek form Messias, transliterates the Hebrew for the anointed. The word appears only twice for the promised prince, in Daniel 9:26 and Psalm 2:2. Yet when a name was wanted for the promised one, at once King and Saviour, this royal synonym served naturally, marking both the King's dignity and his relation to God. The full title Anointed of Jahveh occurs in the Psalms of Solomon and the Apocalypse of Baruch, but the short form was in common use.

 In the Palestine Talmud the form with the article is nearly universal. The Babylonian Talmud's common use without the article is too weak an argument for antiquity to prove it a proper name in Christ's day. The entry proposes three tasks: outline the prophecies of the Messiah, trace their growth in later Judaism, and show how Christ vindicated his right to the title.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-methuselah:
Methuselah, one of the Hebrew patriarchs named in Genesis 5, also appears as Mathusale and Mathusala. Scholars differ on his name's sense. Holzinger offers man of the javelin. Hommel and many others offer man of Selah, Selah being a Babylonian word and title of the god Sin. Sayce traces it to a Babylonian word not understood. Genesis traces his descent through his father Henoch to Seth, a son of Adam and Eve.

 When Methuselah reached one hundred and eighty-seven he became father of Lamech, then lived seven hundred and eighty-two more years, dying at nine hundred and sixty-nine. His death thus fell in the year of the Deluge. No other human is recorded to have lived so long, so Methuselah has become a byword for longevity. Rationalists and advanced critics deny the patriarchs' great ages outright, while Catholic commentators accept Genesis's words without difficulty.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolaus-olah:
Hungarian primate Nicolaus Olah, born at Nagyszeben in 1493, rebuilt church life in a kingdom torn by Turks and reformers. Page at the court of Wladislaw II, then secretary to kings and to Queen Mary, he followed her to the Netherlands in 1531 and stayed a decade.

Back in Hungary in 1542, Olah rose from royal chancellor and bishop of Agram to archbishop of Esztergom in 1553. He crowned kings, founded schools and a seminary, pressed for a learned clergy, and left letters and notes that light up his age. He died in 1568. His autobiographical notes and letters show his crowded career in full.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noah:
Noah, ninth patriarch of the Sethite line and son of Lamech, stands in Genesis as the second father of humankind. His name, tied to rest and comfort, answered his father's hope that the boy would ease the curse laid on the ground after Adam.

Amid a corrupt age, Noah walked with God, built the Ark at divine command, and carried his family and the animals through the Flood. Afterward he planted a vineyard, and the entry weighs his drunkenness, his blessing and curse on his sons, and his 950 years. Commentators read Lamech’s words as hope, prophecy, or a father’s wish for rest in old age.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-savannah:
Savannah, a diocese covering the state of Georgia, was created by Pius IX in 1850. Its first bishop, Francis Xavier Gartland of Philadelphia, was consecrated on 10 September 1850 and died four years later. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia lists a quick succession of bishops in a young southern see.

John Barry of Augusta followed in 1857 and died in 1859. Augustus Verot, vicar apostolic of Florida, succeeded but resigned in 1870 and returned to Florida, dying in 1876. Ignatius Persico, transferred from Charleston in 1870, resigned two years later through ill health. William Gross, consecrated in 1873, moved to Oregon City in 1885, and Thomas Becker, transferred from Wilmington in 1886, died in 1899. Bernard Keiley then took charge.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sophonias-zep:
Sophonias, better known as Zephaniah, was the ninth of the twelve Minor Prophets, preaching in Jerusalem in the second half of the seventh century before Christ. A contemporary and supporter of Jeremiah, he takes his name from a Hebrew word meaning the Lord conceals, or the Lord protects. And his whole surviving work runs to only three short chapters.

His ministry fell under King Josias, after the idolatrous reigns of Amon and Manasse had filled Jerusalem with the cults of Baal and Astarte. The entry draws everything known about him from that brief book, tracing its warnings, its hopes, and its place in the reform that Josias would soon attempt.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-torah:
Torah first means direction or instruction, as a parent's teaching or a wise man's counsel, and chiefly God's instruction through Moses and the prophets. In the sense of law it means only divine laws. The word also names the books holding the Mosaic revelation and law, that is, the Pentateuch, the first five books of the Bible.

In Jewish theology Torah can mean the whole body of Jewish doctrine, whether as a guide for belief and conduct or as a field of study. It can also mean the entire Scriptures, or single passages from Prophets and Writings. The entry then details the Pentateuch itself. It counts 290 open and 379 closed paragraphs, Sabbath lessons on a three-year cycle in Palestine, and 154 to 175 sedarim, or reading sections.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-urmiah:
Urmiah is a residential see in Chaldea, in the Persian province of Adherbaidjan. Its primitive name seems to have been Urmui, or rather Urmedji. It is said, but with little truth, to be the birthplace of Zoroaster, who supposedly lived in a nearby grotto. Nothing is known of its early history. Some wrongly place at Urmiah Bishop John of Persa, present at Nicaea in 325.

The Synodicon of the Chaldean Church makes no mention of Urmiah for several centuries. On the other hand a See of Adherbaidjan existed from 420 to the thirteenth century, suffragan of Arbela. Yet no proof shows its bishop lived at Urmiah rather than elsewhere in the province. The entry sorts these claims with care, leaving Urmiah's early church history largely open.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-utah:
Utah, the thirty-second state admitted to the Union, takes its name from the Ute or Yuta tribe, a Shoshonean people whose hunting grounds covered three-fourths of the state. It measures 350 miles long and 275 miles wide, with an area of 84,990 square miles, of which 2,780 are water. The thirteenth census counted 373,351 people. Nevada bounds it west, Colorado and Wyoming east, Arizona south, and Idaho and Wyoming north.

The Wasatch and Uintah ranges cross the state from north to south, with lesser heights giving variety to basins and valleys. The entry describes its physiography, climate, resources, and people, then turns to church history: the Mormon settlement, the coming of Catholic missionaries, and the diocese's parishes and schools. It offers a full state portrait with a Catholic focus.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-isaiah-and:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on Isaiah and Jeremiah gathers sermons on the two great prophets. Alexander Maclaren expounds Isaiah chapters I to XLVIII in the first part. Jeremiah follows in the same sermon form. Each entry grows from a brief quoted text.

Isaiah entries open with The Great Suit: Jehovah versus Judah. Vision and Service treats the prophet's call in chapter VI. The Kingdom and the King takes up the child of Isaiah IX. Later pieces include The Song of Two Cities and Light or Fire. Maclaren often pairs a striking image with a moral turn. His titles, such as The Sucker from the Felled Oak, show that habit. The volume serves preachers and lay readers alike.
jonah:
Jonah is a novel by Louis Stone about a Sydney larrikin, not the biblical prophet. Its contents divide into two parts, Larrikins All and The Sign of the Silver Shoe. Jonah's world is Cardigan Street, street corners on Saturday night, and the Push, his gang. Early chapters show him eating green peas, discovering a baby, and courting Pinkey.

A quiet wedding follows, and Jonah starts out on his own at Paddy's Market. The second part centers on the Silver Shoe, a family in exile, and Mrs. Partridge lending a hand. Death, a two-up school, and a fatal accident darken the later chapters. Stone writes the rough humor and hard luck of working-class Sydney life in Jonah's story.
little-sarah:
An unknown maker shaped this colored toy book in verse. Little Sarah stands by her grandmother's bed at breakfast time. Grandmother wants a Johnny-cake mixed in one minute flat. It must bake in two minutes more, grandmother insists.

The meal barrel stands empty as wind, Sarah discovers. The shopkeeper sends her running to the miller instead. The miller sends her onward to the cornfield over the hill. Each errand repeats the hurry of the cumulative rhyme. The corn had not grown when Sarah reached the field. Her chain of errands stretches the Johnny-cake's two minutes delightfully.
minnesota-and-dacotah:
C. C. Andrews wrote these letters after touring the Northwest in the autumn of 1856. He was a counselor at law and editor of the official opinions of the attorneys general. The second edition appeared at Washington in 1857. His title page quotes Longfellow's lines about the land of the Ojibways and the Dacotahs.

Andrews describes Minnesota and the Dacotah country for eastern readers. He adds information about public lands and a table of statistics. Such books guided emigrants choosing where to settle in the territories. His letters preserve a lawyer's careful view of the upper Mississippi country just before Minnesota statehood.
tanakh-jps-1917-isaiah:
Isaiah is the longest prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 English Bible. It is called the vision of Isaiah son of Amoz, seen in the days of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Heaven and earth are called to hear a sharp charge: children raised by God have turned away in revolt. Ox and ass know their masters, yet Israel does not know its maker. The land lies waste, towns burn, and Zion sits lone as a booth in a vineyard. Readers get grand verse that swings from blame and ruin to comfort and hope, long prized as the peak of Hebrew prophecy.
tanakh-jps-1917-jeremiah:
Jeremiah is a long prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the Masoretic-based English of the Jewish Publication Society from 1917. Jeremiah is named as son of Hilkiah, of the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin.

His call comes in the thirteenth year of King Josiah and runs through the fall of Jerusalem under Zedekiah. The young man pleads that he is a mere child who cannot speak, but God touches his mouth and sets him over nations. Readers follow a lone voice through siege, grief, and blame, tasked to root out and pull down, yet also to build and to plant.
tanakh-jps-1917-jonah:
Jonah is a short story book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English of the Jewish Publication Society. Jonah son of Amittai is told to go to Nineveh, the great city, and speak out against it.

Rather than obey, Jonah flees by ship, and a great storm rises that threatens to break the vessel apart. The crew cast lots, the lot falls on Jonah, and he tells them to throw him into the sea. Once they do, the sea grows calm, and a great fish swallows him for three days and nights. Readers meet a runaway prophet whose brief tale probes mercy shown even to a foe city.
tanakh-jps-1917-micah:
Micah is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, given in the 1917 English Bible of the Jewish Publication Society. Micah the Morashtite speaks in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, with words about Samaria and Jerusalem.

All peoples are called to hear as God comes down and treads the high places, melting hills like wax. The cause is the sin of Jacob, pinned on Samaria's idols and Jerusalem's high places alike. Micah warns that carved images will be smashed and the city made a heap. Readers meet bold verse that blasts rich abuse of the poor, yet also holds a famed hope for peace among nations.
tanakh-jps-1917-nehemiah:
Nehemiah is a history book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the 1917 Jewish Publication Society version of the Holy Scriptures. Nehemiah serves as cupbearer to King Artaxerxes of Persia when word of Jerusalem's ruin reaches him.

He prays in grief for his people's sins, then waits for a chance to speak to the king. In the month Nisan, the king notes his sad face and asks what he needs. Nehemiah asks to be sent to Judah to rebuild the city of his fathers' tombs, and gains royal letters and timber. Readers follow wall building under threat, debt relief, and a renewed pledge to the law in a small, weak province.
tanakh-jps-1917-obadiah:
Obadiah is the shortest book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society English of 1917. It is called the vision of Obadiah, and its whole word is aimed at Edom, Israel's old foe and kin.

A report from God has been heard, and a herald sent among the nations to rise up against Edom in war. Edom is charged with pride in its rock strongholds and with standing aloof when Jerusalem fell. The book warns that as Edom has done, so it shall be done in return. Readers get one sharp chapter of judgment, paired with a close that gives Mount Zion to those who escape and the kingdom to God.
tanakh-jps-1917-zechariah:
Zechariah is a long book among the short prophets, presented in the Jewish Publication Society translation of 1917. Zechariah son of Berechiah is placed in the second year of Darius, king of Persia, after the return from exile.

God tells the people that he was sore displeased with their fathers, who shut their ears to past prophets. He calls this new age group to turn back to him so that he will turn back to them. Soon Zechariah sees a night vision of a man among trees. Readers get strange visions of horses, horns, and a flying scroll, plus clear calls to rebuild the temple and live justly.
tanakh-jps-1917-zephaniah:
Zephaniah is a short prophetic book of the Hebrew Bible, here in the Jewish Publication Society rendering of 1917. Zephaniah son of Cushi speaks in the days of Josiah son of Amon, king of Judah.

His word is stark: God will sweep all things from the face of the earth, man and beast, birds and fish alike. Judah and Jerusalem face the cut for Baal worship, roof-top star rites, and mixed oaths sworn to two gods at once. Readers get a grim day-of-the-Lord warning in three short chapters, which still ends with song, as God is said to rejoice over a cleansed and gathered people.
the-american-goliah:
A pamphlet from 1869, billed as the only authorized account from the owners, tells of a stone giant dug up in Onondaga County, New York. The find, dated October 16, 1869, is said to be a perfectly formed man ten and one-half feet high. Its sellers, Redington and Howe, promise fresh facts and expert views as they appear.

Boosters call the stone figure perhaps the greatest find of the century in this country. The pages gather witness statements taken on the spot, press reports, and the views of learned men on the supposed petrified body. Cuts showing points of interest were still being prepared when this early issue went out.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-16-neh:
Nehemiah , read in the King James Version, begins with the words of Nehemiah, son of Hachaliah, at Shushan the palace in the month Chisleu, in a twentieth year. Hanani, one of his brethren, arrives with men from Judah.

Nehemiah asks about the Jews left from captivity and about Jerusalem. The answer is grim: the remnant is in great affliction and reproach, the wall is broken down, and its gates are burned with fire. Hearing it, Nehemiah sits, weeps, mourns for days, fasts, and prays. His prayer confesses Israel's sins as well as his father's house.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-23-isa:
Isaiah , given here in King James English, opens with a vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz, concerning Judah and Jerusalem. It is dated to the reigns of Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah.

Heavens and earth are called to hear, for God says he raised children who rebelled. An ox knows its owner and an ass its master's crib, but Israel does not consider. The nation is called sinful, laden with iniquity, and sick from head to foot, with wounds and sores. Charge and lament open a long prophetic book aimed at a people who have forsaken their God.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-24-jer:
Jeremiah in the authorised King James wording, opens with the words of Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, from the priests at Anathoth in Benjamin. God's word came to him in the thirteenth year of Josiah and continued through Jehoiakim to Zedekiah's eleventh year, when Jerusalem was carried captive.

Before I formed thee I knew thee, God tells him, ordaining him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah protests that he is a child who cannot speak. God answers that he must go where sent and say what is commanded. Calling, fear, and a long span ending in exile frame the book.
the-bible-king-james-version-book-38-zec:
Zechariah in the King James text, starts in the eighth month of Darius's second year. The word comes to Zechariah, son of Berechiah, son of Iddo the prophet.

God has been sore displeased with your fathers, the message begins. Turn to me, says the Lord of hosts, and I will turn to you. Do not be like the fathers, who heard former prophets cry for a turn from evil ways and would not listen. Where are those fathers now, Zechariah asks, and do prophets live forever? Return after exile, urged through a dead generation's failure, opens the book.
the-circus-boys-on-the-plains-or-the-you: The Young Advance Agents Ahead of the Show is the subtitle Edgar B. P. Darlington gave this Circus Boys tale of work on the plains. Greg Berckes prepared the Gutenberg text, released in January 2001 as etext 2478. A standard Gutenberg header fills the whole of what is present. No advance-agent chapter follows it, so the boys' work ahead of the show goes undescribed here.
the-garden-of-allah:
Robert Hichens wrote The Garden of Allah as a novel of the Algerian desert, first printed in 1904. Three books divide the tale: a prelude, the voice of prayer, and the garden itself.

Hichens sets a disgraced monk and a young English woman on a path through the sands, where faith lost and found drives each scene. The desert works on both like a vast church, stripping wealth and rank to bare soul. The book made Hichens famed in his day for lush scenes of sand, palms, and prayer, and for a love tale crossed by vows no priest can loose.
the-world-english-bible-web-isaiah:
Book twenty-three in the World English Bible presents the vision of Isaiah, son of Amoz. He prophesies about Judah and Jerusalem under four kings. Heaven and earth are summoned to listen. God says he raised children who rebelled against him. Even an ox knows its owner, Isaiah laments. Israel, by contrast, does not consider its master.

The nation is called sinful and loaded with iniquity. Its whole head is sick, its heart faint. Wounds and open sores cover it, the prophet says. Why invite more beating by revolting further, he asks. Judgment opens the book, yet promises of restoration follow. Isaiah shapes later faith with unmatched poetic power.
the-world-english-bible-web-jeremiah:
Jeremiah's words form book twenty-four in the World English Bible. He is Hilkiah's son, from a priestly family in Anathoth. God's word first came to him under King Josiah. His ministry ran through Jehoiakim's reign to Zedekiah's end. It closed when Jerusalem was carried away captive. Jeremiah then recalls his call as a young man.

God says he knew Jeremiah before forming him in the womb. He was appointed a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah protests that he is only a child who cannot speak. God rejects the excuse and sends him anyway. Readers follow a reluctant prophet through decades of unwelcome warnings.
the-world-english-bible-web-micah:
Micah speaks in book thirty-three of the World English Bible, a prophet from Moresheth. His word comes under kings Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Samaria and Jerusalem both fall under his gaze. All peoples are told to hear his warning. God himself will witness against them from his temple. He comes down and treads the earth's high places.

Mountains melt under him like wax before fire. Valleys split like water poured down a slope. Jacob's disobedience, Micah says, causes this judgment. Samaria will become a rubble heap in the field. Later chapters promise a ruler from Bethlehem. Readers hear fierce justice joined with surprising hope for the humble.
the-world-english-bible-web-nehemiah:
Book sixteen in the World English Bible gives the words of Nehemiah, son of Hacaliah. He is at the palace in Shushan during the month Chislev. His brother Hanani arrives with men from Judah. Nehemiah asks about Jews who survived the captivity. Their report is grim: the remnant suffers great affliction. Jerusalem's wall lies broken and its gates burned.

Hearing this, Nehemiah sits down and weeps. He mourns for days, fasting and praying. His prayer calls God great and awesome. Covenant mercy for those who love God anchors his plea. A cupbearer will soon rebuild a city. Readers watch prayer turn into organized, risky action.
the-world-english-bible-web-zechariah:
Zechariah prophesies in book thirty-eight of the World English Bible, during Darius' second year. He is Berechiah's son and Iddo's grandson. God's opening word recalls anger at Israel's fathers. Earlier prophets urged repentance, but the fathers would not listen. Now God calls the new generation back to him. He promises to come back to them in turn.

The fathers are gone, Zechariah notes, and prophets do not live forever. God's words, though, overtook that older generation. Night visions of horsemen, horns, and a flying scroll follow. A restored Jerusalem and a coming king fill later chapters. Post-exile hope takes strange, vivid shapes here.
